You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

– the failing test (signature + snippet),

Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test `testAddNonComparable` is designed to verify that adding a non-comparable object to a `Frequency` instance should throw a `ClassCastException`. However, the test shows that the call to `addValue(new Object())` did not throw `ClassCastException` as expected, implying the method allowed adding a plain `Object` (non-comparable). This is problematic because the `Frequency` class internally uses a `TreeMap` (`freqTable`) which requires all keys to be mutually comparable. Adding a plain `Object` not implementing `Comparable` can cause issues when further values are added, potentially leading to an inconsistent state or throwing `IllegalArgumentException` on subsequent inserts.

Looking at the `Frequency.addValue(Object v)` method, it directly accepts an `Object` as an argument, with the stated contract that if other objects have already been added, `v` must be comparable to those. The method checks if the input is an `Integer` and converts it to `Long`, then it tries to get the count from `freqTable` and update it accordingly. It catches a `ClassCastException` which would be thrown by the `TreeMap` if comparisons are not possible, and rethrows it as an `IllegalArgumentException`.

However, the initial addition of an arbitrary `Object` (non-comparable) does not throw a `ClassCastException` because there is no comparison at that point (the object is simply put into the map). The first object stored becomes the key with no problem, but subsequent additions try to compare keys which may lead to runtime exceptions.

Thus, the bug is that `addValue(Object)` does not enforce the argument type to be `Comparable`. It should directly check if the incoming value is `Comparable` and fail early if not, to prevent adding incompatible keys. This matches the current bug report that the initial call allows a plain `Object` to be added which later breaks the `Frequency` instance.

The related recent bug reports on `Frequency` mention ambiguity about what can be added, but none explicitly address the issue of enforcing comparable types.

Root cause: The method `addValue(Object)` accepts any `Object` without verifying it implements `Comparable`, which breaks the expectation and causes unstable behavior in the `Frequency` class using a `TreeMap`.

Recommended fix locations: add explicit type and comparability checks in `Frequency.addValue(Object)` to forbid adding non-comparable Objects.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
